candidateRows: A causal series must have a first cause if it has neither an infinite regress nor a closed causal loop.
This deduction supplies the first-cause stage on which every later inference to a beginningless personal creator depends.
Loke introduces a causal series, exhausts the alternatives as infinite regress, closed loop, or first cause, and states that excluding the first two yields the third.
The first cause is beginningless and initially changeless because whatever begins has a cause and every change is a beginning event.
The move derives two defining properties needed to distinguish the proposed first cause from the Big Bang and other beginning events.
Loke invokes the causal principle, defines changes as events with beginnings, excludes an event such as the Big Bang from being first, and concludes initial changelessness.
An initially changeless first cause must be transcendent and immaterial rather than a constantly changing material or quantum system.
This inference advances the argument from a generic first cause toward the nonphysical creator described by the debate motion.
Loke characterizes transcendence as beyond ordinary experience and argues that material and quantum systems constantly change, unlike the initially changeless first cause.
Originating an event without prior determination while retaining the capacity not to change requires libertarian freedom and therefore personal agency.
This is the principal bridge from an initially changeless first cause to the personal creator asserted in the motion.
Loke says the first cause must initiate an event by itself yet be able to remain changeless; he identifies this dual capacity as libertarian freedom implying an agent.
Several independent arguments can exclude an infinite causal regress, so defending even one successful argument is sufficient for the first-cause case.
Excluding infinite regress is one of Loke's identified crucial premises, and this move states his cumulative and independent defense strategy.
Loke lists Hilbert's Hotel, traversal, dependence-regress, Grim Reaper, and Methuselah-style arguments, claims any one would suffice, and selects his novel dependence argument.
Merely asserting an argument's premises makes no epistemic progress beyond asserting its conclusion unless the premises receive an adequate status or defense.
The objection challenges whether Loke's deductive presentation can establish its conclusion rather than simply relocating the disputed assertion.
Loke's presentation of a valid deductive route from its stated premises to a personal creator.
Oppy asks for the discussion's ground rules and argues that replacing a bare conclusion with disputed premises does not advance the case without explaining their epistemic standing.
Successive supporting arguments threaten a regress of disputed premises, potentially ending with claims whose standing is no better than the original conclusion.
The move presses the methodological objection against Loke's planned premise defenses and asks what could provide a satisfactory stopping point.
Loke's proposal to defend the causal principle and impossibility of infinite regress through further subarguments.
Oppy argues that each subargument introduces new premises that may also be rejected, producing a looming regress unless some premises become genuinely irresistible.
Theory is prior to argument because a person's accepted theory determines which premises and arguments they regard as true or sound.
This supplies Oppy's overarching framework for resisting premise-by-premise proof and reframes the debate as comparison of whole theories.
Loke's proposed method of establishing premises by offering reasons and rebutting alternative possibilities.
Oppy says theories determine attitudes toward premises; arguments chiefly expose inconsistency or uncomfortable consequences, while abstract soundness is not the proper primary focus.
Causation is fundamentally a relation between events, while talk of things as causes is a legitimate but derivative description.
Clarifying the relata of causation is necessary for evaluating Loke's series, his treatment of changes, and the proposed first cause.
Loke's first premise asserting a series of causes, effects, and changes without yet fixing the causal relata.
Oppy contrasts event and thing causation, explains their interdefinability through changing properties, and states that event causation is more fundamental though thing causation remains acceptable.
The shared premise that causal reality exists remains contestable because agreement between the debaters does not answer causal skeptics.
The observation limits what the agreed first premise establishes and identifies an undefended assumption at the foundation of Loke's argument.
The jointly accepted first premise that there is a causal network of items related as causes and effects.
Oppy accepts causal reality for the discussion but notes that skeptics reject it and that the participants have offered nothing here to persuade them.
The exclusion of causal loops follows only from irreflexivity plus a controversial transitivity principle, leaving dissenters unconvinced.
The move identifies the assumptions required to exclude causal loops, a necessary step in deriving first causes from the proposed causal structure.
Loke's presentation of causal loops as excluded by the agreed causal premises.
After agreement on causal reality, Oppy distinguishes agreement within the debate from justification for observers who reject transitivity or permit causal loops.
A causal loop need not constitute a vicious regress because each member can occur once rather than recur infinitely.
The distinction challenges a specific rationale for excluding causal loops and clarifies that looping dependence is not automatically infinite recurrence.
Loke's claim that a closed causal loop necessarily involves a vicious regress.
Loke appeals to a book-length argument treating causal loops as vicious; Oppy responds by separating a single closed sequence from repeated infinite occurrence.
Dynamic causal loops involve infinite regress, while static loops involve vicious circular dependence in which each beginning ultimately depends on itself.
The move supplies the distinction needed to preserve Loke's objection after Oppy denies that every causal loop repeats its events infinitely.
Oppy's distinction between a causal loop and an infinitely recurring sequence.
Oppy argues that members of a loop occur only once; Loke answers by assigning different defects to dynamic and static forms of looping causation.
Although a causal infinite regress is probably absent and would be impossible if absent, belief in its possibility or actuality can remain rational.
The move separates agreement on the likely conclusion from disagreement about whether Loke's arguments establish that conclusion with sufficient force.
Loke's use of Oppy's writings as support for rejecting an infinite causal regress.
Oppy clarifies that his own preferred view excludes infinite regress but that he regards competing views about its possibility and actuality as reasonable.
The shared causal premises establish at least one uncaused cause but do not establish that exactly one first cause exists.
The move limits what the agreed first-stage premises entail and identifies an additional uniqueness premise needed for a single-creator conclusion.
Loke's formulation of the conclusion as there being a first cause treated as unique.
Following agreement about loops and regress, Oppy reconstructs the inference to first causes and highlights ambiguity between at least one and exactly one.
The causal principle matters because it entails that any first cause has no beginning, thereby supporting properties attributed to the creator.
The move connects the disputed causal principle to the motion's beginningless-creator conclusion rather than merely to the existence of some first cause.
A request for relevance follows the derivation of first causes; Loke explains that the principle is needed to infer that the first cause never began.
The argument requires only at least one creator; uniqueness would depend on separate considerations such as simplicity, physical-law uniformity, or revelation.
The clarification fixes the intended quantifier of the conclusion and prevents the reformulated Kalam from carrying an unsupported uniqueness commitment.
Oppy's objection that Loke's first-cause conclusion shifts ambiguously from at least one cause to exactly one.
After explaining the causal principle's role, Loke concedes that this argument establishes only one-or-more creators and brackets independent arguments for uniqueness.
A necessary initial natural state can explain the universe's beginning without a cause, while every later existent or occurrence remains causally explained.
The proposal supplies the principal naturalistic rival to a beginningless creator by replacing universal causal explanation with universal explanation simpliciter.
Loke's principle that whatever begins to exist must have a cause.
Oppy treats the initial universe and its initial expansion as necessary, causeless but explained, while restricting causal requirements to non-initial reality.
If the universe began uncaused, no prior constraint would distinguish it from other possible beginnings, so unobserved spontaneous universes and events should also arise.
This is a sustained argument for the disputed causal principle that is required to infer a beginningless first cause rather than a necessary initial universe.
Oppy's account of the initial natural state as necessary, explained, and uncaused.
Loke argues from the apparent absence of unconstrained spontaneous beginnings: an uncaused universe would remove relevant differences preventing many comparable beginnings.
On the necessary-initial-state view, nothing can enter natural reality except through the initial state or its causal evolution, and Loke gives no reason to prefer necessary God.
The reply blocks the predicted proliferation of uncaused entities and argues that the observation does not discriminate between rival necessary foundations.
Loke's claim that an uncaused universe would imply unconstrained spontaneous beginnings throughout natural reality.
Oppy answers that his theory necessarily restricts natural reality to an initial state and subsequent causal development, then denies any comparative advantage for God.
An uncaused initial state with a beginning cannot be necessary, because the causal argument rules out its uniquely beginning without a cause.
This directly defends the causal principle against Oppy's necessary-initial-state alternative and therefore bears on whether a creator is explanatorily required.
Oppy's claim that the universe's initial state and expansion may exist metaphysically necessarily without a cause.
Oppy had proposed a necessary initial natural state as a rival to necessary divine creation; Loke answers that a beginning initial state cannot uniquely be uncaused.
Without a cause selecting among logically possible universes, rival possibilities would be equally actualized, so Oppy's naturalistic initial-state proposal does not defeat the argument.
It supplies the modal discrimination premise intended to show that an unexplained natural initial state cannot account for this universe rather than alternatives.
Oppy's proposal to treat the universe as exhausting natural reality and its initial state as necessary.
After addressing whether the initial state can be uncaused, Loke distinguishes the actual universe from other logical possibilities and argues that selection requires a cause.
A beginningless God is exempt from the causal principle and, as an intelligent free cause, can explain the universe's highly ordered and fine-tuned character.
The move both blocks a causal regress objection to God and advances the proposed personal creator as explanatorily superior to the naturalistic rival.
Oppy's comparison between a necessarily existing God and a necessarily existing initial state of the universe.
Loke argues that the causal principle applies only to what begins and then claims that an intelligent divine cause explains order and fine-tuning unavailable to Oppy's theory.
Fine-tuning need not be brutally contingent because, if fixed in a necessarily existing initial state, its values could not have been otherwise.
This neutralizes Loke's claimed explanatory advantage for an intelligent creator by locating the constants' explanation in the necessary initial natural state.
Loke's claim that only an intelligent divine cause can explain why the universe is highly ordered and fine-tuned.
Oppy responds that his view does not posit brute contingent fine-tuning: when constants are fixed initially, their values inherit the necessity of that state.
Beginninglessness need not involve an infinite regress, because a timeless and initially changeless being has no finite temporal extent and therefore no temporal beginning.
This is the principal defense of the argument's claimed beginningless creator against the charge that beginninglessness restores the infinite regress rejected earlier.
Oppy's objection that a beginningless God entails states without a first member and therefore an infinite regress.
After Oppy argues that any earlier state requires another earlier state, Loke distinguishes temporal regress from timeless existence and defines beginning by finite temporal extent.
Changelessness requires an extension over which no change occurs, leaving Loke with either an infinite regress or a finite duration that has a beginning.
It challenges the coherence of the beginningless divine state at the heart of the motion and argues that neither available interpretation preserves Loke's conclusion.
Loke's claim that God can be timeless, initially changeless, and beginningless without an infinite temporal regress.
Oppy contends that changelessness cannot describe a single unextended point; once extension is admitted, it must be finite or infinite, defeating beginninglessness either way.
If change, beginning, and measurement are inapplicable to a dimensionless God, calling God beginningless or changeless cannot perform the argumentative work Loke requires.
This attacks the semantic coherence of the exemption that protects God from the causal principle, potentially removing the basis for the creator's asserted beginninglessness.
Loke's claim that God exists beyond every dimension and is therefore changeless without occupying a point or duration.
Oppy argues that predicates cannot establish a privileged value when their governing dimension is wholly inapplicable, comparing beginninglessness with an invalid zero-measure attribution.
A timeless causal order still must contain either one point or multiple ordered stages, and a single divine stage would itself constitute an absolute causal beginning.
It reframes the temporal dispute in causal rather than temporal terms and argues that Loke has not established a genuinely beginningless creator in the relevant order.
Loke's proposal that God is first in a non-temporal causal order and thus marks an absolute origin without beginning in time.
Accepting that time starts with the universe, Oppy asks what structures the allegedly prior causal order and argues that one divine member amounts to a beginning.
God can exist timelessly and changelessly without the universe and enter time with creation, while the timeless divine state is neither a temporal point nor an extension.
This supplies the positive metaphysical model meant to reconcile divine causal priority with the absence of a temporal beginning or an infinite temporal regress.
Oppy's demand that Loke specify whether God's pre-universe causal order contains one point, many points, or an infinite regress.
Loke clarifies that God exists without time before creation and in time with creation, rejecting the premise that the timeless condition must be modeled as points.
The necessary-initial-universe theory explains the same facts with fewer entities, while adding God provides no compensating explanatory advantage over the naturalistic account.
This is a direct comparative verdict on the motion's rival explanations, invoking simplicity and explanatory parity to deny that Loke's creator hypothesis succeeds.
Loke's contention that a timeless personal God coherently causes the contingent universe and improves its explanation.
Oppy compares the proposals by necessity, causal and explanatory principles, explanatory coverage, and ontological economy, concluding that God is an idle addition.
Loke's modus tollens argument rules out an uncaused beginning of the initial state unless one of its premises is successfully denied.
The move directly defends the causal principle that underpins the reformulated Kalam by claiming a deductive exclusion of an uncaused initial state.
Oppy's comparison claiming that the naturalist theory is simpler while matching theism's explanatory power.
Oppy had characterized God as an idle explanatory addition; Loke answers that his deductive premises, rather than simplicity alone, exclude Oppy's initial-state account.
The initial state exists necessarily, while every contingent later thing has a cause, so contingent entities cannot simply appear uncaused.
This move supplies Oppy's governing method for rejecting Loke's premise: compare complete theories by simplicity and explanatory adequacy unless inconsistency is derived.
Loke's claim that Oppy supplied no proof for treating the initial state as necessary and rejecting the first premise.
Oppy says theory choice controls premise acceptance: his necessary initial state explains the same relevant data with fewer commitments, absent a demonstrated contradiction.
If anything begins uncaused, no cause, intrinsic difference, or surrounding circumstance can restrict uncaused beginnings to that thing alone.
The move states the principal support for Loke's causal premise and argues that Oppy's appeal to necessity has not answered the three underlying reasons.
Oppy's rejection of the first causal premise through the asserted necessity of the universe's initial state.
Prompted to clarify the premise, Loke gives three reasons why one uncaused beginning would imply other possible uncaused beginnings and challenges Oppy's necessity response.
A necessary initial state is explained by its necessity, whereas every non-initial state falls under a causal principle and cannot arise uncaused.
The distinction between necessary initial reality and caused non-initial reality is the core naturalist alternative to Loke's unrestricted causal principle.
Loke's contention that an uncaused initial state leaves room for other things to begin without causes.
Oppy combines a universal explanatory principle with a causal principle for non-initial things, maintaining that necessity explains the initial state and excludes rivals.
Disagreement over premises must be resolved through comparative theoretical virtues or a derived contradiction, not by merely restating consequences rejected by the rival theory.
This methodological move determines what could rationally decide the dispute and specifies simplicity, explanatory reach, and consistency as available routes.
Loke's assertion that his three reasons show Oppy's necessary-initial-state assumption to be mistaken.
Oppy argues that Loke cannot advance the debate simply by insisting on claims denied by Oppy's theory; a comparative virtue or contradiction is required.
Any property distinguishing the initial state can exist only once that state exists, making the property explanatorily vacuous regarding its uncaused beginning.
The move attacks necessity as an explanation of the initial state by arguing that its differentiating property arrives too late to explain the state's beginning.
Oppy's claim that the initial state differs from later uncaused candidates because the initial state is necessary.
Loke accepts that Oppy labels the initial state special but argues that any special property presupposes the state's existence and cannot explain its beginning.
No special property of the initial state can explain why only it begins uncaused, and deductive analysis of an uncaused beginning therefore falsifies Oppy's theory.
The extended move develops both the explanatory-vacuity objection and Loke's claim that his understanding of uncaused beginning deductively entails Oppy's theory is false.
Oppy's insistence that necessity is a substantive explanation and rules out every incompatible alternative initial state.
Across a brief non-debate interruption, Loke develops why a state's own property cannot explain its beginning and grounds his contrary conclusion in purportedly analytic premises.
The best modal theory makes every possible world share an initial history, rendering the actual initial state necessarily first and excluding alternatives.
The move supplies positive modal grounds for the initial state's necessity rather than treating necessity as an unexplained property attached after the state exists.
Loke's argument that a special property cannot explain or differentiate an initial state until that state already exists.
Oppy explains necessity through a modal theory on which worlds share an initial history and diverge only through later chance outcomes, excluding rival beginnings.
Alternative logically consistent universes remain available, and no property possessed only after this universe exists can explain why this possibility alone is actualized.
The move presses the principal pro-side objection against Oppy's modal account by demanding a non-circular differentiator among consistent candidate initial universes.
Oppy's assertion that metaphysical necessity leaves no alternative whatsoever to the actual initial state.
Loke distinguishes logical alternatives from the actualized universe and argues that any differentiating property presupposes actuality, leaving necessity explanatorily superfluous.
Logical consistency does not establish metaphysical possibility, so consistent descriptions of alternative universes do not undermine the initial state's metaphysical necessity.
The reply blocks Loke's appeal to conceivable alternatives by distinguishing logical consistency from the stronger metaphysical modality asserted by Oppy's theory.
Loke's appeal to logically possible alternative universes as evidence that the actual initial state is not necessary.
Oppy grants that alternative consistent stories can be told but denies that they are metaphysically possible, illustrating the distinction through modal-theistic reasoning.
Oppy's metaphysical theory fails because no special property explains the initial state, whereas God's beginninglessness explains the relevant necessity.
This challenges the explanatory adequacy of the principal naturalistic rival while defending the creator hypothesis against the same modal objection.
Oppy's claim that metaphysical necessity can characterize the initial state without a further special explanatory property.

Oppy had distinguished metaphysical possibility from mere logical consistency; Loke answers that the naturalistic initial state remains explanatorily unsupported while beginninglessness supports God's necessity.
Necessity itself is the special property of the initial state, and ultimate explanations of necessity must terminate in something unexplained.
The move supplies the naturalist theory's stopping point and directly contests Loke's demand for a deeper explanation of the initial state's necessity.
Loke's objection that Oppy's initial state needs a special property capable of explaining why it exists necessarily.
After Loke says no property can do the required work, Oppy identifies necessity as the property and argues that unexplained necessity is a legitimate ultimate explanatory terminus.
Derived necessities may be explained by other necessities, but the explanatory chain must ultimately ground out in necessities having no further explanation.
This qualification establishes the regress-stopping principle supporting Oppy's defense of an unexplained metaphysically necessary initial condition.
Loke's contention that necessary realities can still have explanations of why they possess their necessity.
The moderator isolates a disagreement over whether necessity can be explained; Oppy concedes derivative explanations while insisting that ultimate necessity remains unexplained.
Existing at every time in the actual world does not entail existing necessarily, so the inference from beginninglessness to necessity is invalid.
The objection attacks Loke's stated reason for treating the beginningless divine cause as necessary and therefore undercuts an important claimed advantage over naturalism.
Loke's claim that something which has no beginning always exists and therefore exists necessarily.
Loke grounds God's necessity in beginninglessness; Oppy responds that always existing within the actual world and existing across possible worlds are distinct claims.
Possible-world semantics demonstrates that an entity can always exist in this world yet fail to exist in another, defeating the move from always to necessarily.
The countermodel gives substantive modal support for Oppy's objection and challenges Loke's justification for assigning necessity to the proposed creator.
Loke's revised assertion that a beginningless, unsustained being cannot fail to exist and is therefore noncontingent.
Oppy explains possibility and necessity using possible worlds, then notes that actual-world persistence leaves open termination or absence in another world.
The relevant necessity is not logical necessity across all worlds but the inability of a beginningless, unsustained first cause to fail to exist in its initial state.
This narrows Loke's modal conclusion to resist Oppy's countermodel while preserving the claimed explanatory contrast between God and a contingent initial state.
Oppy's possible-world objection that actual-world beginninglessness cannot establish existence in every possible world.
Following Oppy's modal countermodel, Loke denies claiming logical necessity and instead appeals to the first cause's beginningless and unsustained initial existence.
A beginningless first cause must initially be changeless yet able both to originate an undetermined event and refrain from changing, which entails libertarian freedom and personhood.
This is the direct inferential bridge from a first cause to a personal agent, addressing the motion's central claim that the creator is personal.
The discussion shifts from the causal principle to Loke's personhood inference; he derives initial changelessness, origination capacity, self-restraint, libertarian freedom, and agency.
Accepting that whatever begins has a cause does not favor a beginningless first cause, because a nonbeliever may more plausibly accept an infinite causal regress.
The move denies that the causal principle alone reaches Loke's required first cause and identifies a major unargued naturalistic alternative.
Loke's derivation of a beginningless first cause from the causal principle that whatever begins to exist has a cause.
Asked where he disagrees with the personhood argument, Oppy first observes that the argument has not excluded an infinite regress and temporarily brackets that dispute.
An instantaneous event occurring wholly at the universe's initial time need not possess a distinct beginning, undermining the claim that every event begins.
The objection challenges the premise that makes the first cause non-eventful and initially changeless, thereby threatening the later inference to libertarian agency.
Loke's premise that events necessarily have beginnings and that the beginningless first cause therefore cannot itself be an event.
After setting infinite regress aside, Oppy considers expansion at the initial instant and argues that an event wholly occurring then lacks a separable beginning.
Beginning means being finite in the earlier-than direction, not having a distinct beginning point, so even an initial instantaneous event falls under the causal principle.
This reply defends the event-beginning premise required to infer an initially changeless first cause and ultimately a personal originator.
Oppy's objection that an event occurring wholly at the initial instant has no distinct beginning and escapes the causal principle.
Oppy challenges the beginning of an instantaneous initial event; Loke answers with a directional-finitude definition that does not require a first point.
A state can exist without a beginning and later undergo an initial change, whereas an event is itself a change.
The distinction supplies the ontology needed for Loke's account of a beginningless first cause that initiates change without a prior event.
Oppy's request for clarification about what Loke means by a state and how states differ from events.
In his closing statement, Loke revisits Oppy's concern about introducing states and defines their role in the proposed causal account.
No allegedly special property of an initial spacetime block can explain its privileged causal status, because differentiating properties are possessed only once their bearers exist.
This directly challenges the naturalist alternative's explanation of the initial state and supports the causal principle underlying Loke's creator inference.
Oppy's position that the initial state is necessarily existent or otherwise special enough to ground his naturalist theory.
Loke identifies the causal principle as the central disagreement and argues that Oppy's initial-state proposal cannot provide the required explanatory work.
If the causal principle and the argument's remaining premises are true, its valid deductive form makes the existence of a creator a necessary conclusion.
The move explicitly connects the disputed premises and deductive validity to the debate's ultimate conclusion that a creator of the universe exists.
After defending the causal principle against Oppy's alternative, Loke restates the conditional deductive route from his premises to a creator.
Although Loke's assumptions entail a first cause outside the universe, Oppy's own assumptions equally entail a first cause that belongs to the universe.
The parity claim denies that the shared first-cause inference uniquely favors a transcendent creator over Oppy's universe-internal naturalist alternative.
Loke's closing claim that satisfaction of his premises and causal principle deductively establishes a creator outside the universe.
Oppy answers Loke's final inference by contrasting what follows from their respective assumptions and denying that Loke's conclusion has unique support.
